extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners (Office personnel) and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making and documenting obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103 (KSR/Graham framework) during patent examination, including what factual findings, searches, rationales, and applicant responses are required. Intended to direct Office personnel on proper procedures and reasoning to support rejections and to guide consideration of applicant rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the scope and content of the prior art, Office personnel must first obtain a thorough understanding of the invention disclosed and claimed by reading the specification, including the claims, and must determine what to search for and where to search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed (MPEP § 904.02). Follow general search guidelines (MPEP § 904–904.03). Prior art for § 103 may be in the inventor's field or reasonably pertinent (analogous art); see MPEP § 2141.01(a) and § 1504.03 for design applications. A preferred search will look for references that provide a teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine if such references exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must interpret the claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art as a whole to ascertain differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting claim language should follow MPEP § 2111 and the analysis in MPEP § 2141.02. The examiner must consider the entire prior art and claimed invention when identifying the distinctions relied upon in an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness rejection should include, either explicitly or implicitly in view of the prior art applied, an indication of the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: type of problems encountered; prior art solutions; rapidity of innovations; sophistication of technology; educational level of active workers (In re GPAC). Office personnel may rely on their own technical expertise. A finding as to level of skill may be used as a partial basis for the obviousness resolution (see MPEP § 2141.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and evaluation of secondary considerations (objective evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to obviousness—often termed 'secondary considerations'—must be evaluated and may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be in the specification, submitted with the application, or timely provided during prosecution; weight given is case-by-case. Presentation of evidence does not make it dispositive; examiners must assess weight and relevance (Graham factors). See MPEP § 2145 for consideration of rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation of factual findings and reasoned explanation supporting an obviousness rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious; rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning state of the art and teachings of applied references and must provide an explanation (rationale) linking those facts to the legal conclusion (Kahn/KSR). Examiners should explicitly state findings and rationale so applicant can respond (35 U.S.C. 132). Failure to articulate reasoning is an error; simply asserting lack of documentation is insufficient as a traverse by applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense and ordinary creativity (limited and evidence-supported)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense and inferences by a person of ordinary skill may be invoked to supply missing limitations or to combine teachings, but such use must be supported by evidence and reasoned explanation, especially when the missing limitation is central to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR permits a flexible approach including common sense, but the Federal Circuit requires supporting evidence and reasoned explanation (see Arendi, Perfect Web). Examiners may rely on general knowledge in the art but must avoid conclusory leaps and should explain why such inferences would have been made by a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable rationales to support a conclusion of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel may rely on multiple rationales to support an obviousness rejection; the MPEP lists several non-exclusive rationales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of rationales (as listed) include: (A) combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) using a known technique to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a ready-for-improvement device to yield predictable results; (E) 'obvious to try' where finite, predictable solutions exist with reasonable expectation of success; (F) variations prompted by design incentives or market forces across fields when predictable; (G) some teaching/suggestion/motivation in the prior art leading one to modify or combine references. See MPEP § 2143 and § 2144 for examples and illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching‑Suggestion‑Motivation (TSM) rationale is permissible but not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Graham inquiries reveal a prima facie case using the TSM rationale, such a rejection is appropriate; KSR cautions against rigidly requiring TSM but recognizes it as a valid rationale among others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSM 'captured a helpful insight' and is consistent with Graham; however, examiners should not limit themselves to formalistic TSM proofs if other reasoned rationales apply. When relying on TSM, explain how the prior art supplies the teaching, suggestion, or motivation (KSR, Intel v. Qualcomm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art / prior art from other fields may be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is not limited to the inventor's specific field; art in other fields that is reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed may be considered when evaluating obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR emphasized that work available in one field can prompt predictable variations in another; examiners should consider whether references outside the inventor's field would have been reasonably pertinent. See MPEP § 2141.01(a) and § 1504.03 for design applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: give claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim scope determination guides what to search and what prior art to apply; see Phillips v. AWH and MPEP § 2111. Accurate claim interpretation is foundational to identifying differences from prior art and to articulating factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for and where to search
rubrics_metrics.description: Search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed; prior art may be in the field of the inventor’s endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the problem the inventor addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred search looks for references providing teaching/suggestion/motivation if present. Follow MPEP § 904–904.03 for search practice; consult §§ 901–901.06 and §§ 2121–2129 for what constitutes prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant time for obviousness analysis (effective filing date vs. time of invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications subject to first inventor to file (AIA), the relevant time is 'before the effective filing date of the claimed invention'; for pre‑AIA law, the relevant time is 'at the time of the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the appropriate temporal standard when resolving Graham inquiries and evaluating prior art and common knowledge. See MPEP § 2150 et seq. for further timing guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper reply must present reasoned arguments pointing out specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. Mere statements that the Office hasn't established a prima facie case or that common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence are inadequate (and may permit the examiner to repeat the rejection or make it final). See MPEP § 706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence and reconsideration of the rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating an obviousness determination and reconsider initial conclusions in view of the entire record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations and evidence demonstrating: (A) inability of a person of ordinary skill to combine elements by known methods (technological difficulties); (B) that elements in combination do not merely perform the same functions; or (C) that the results were unexpected. After rebuttal, review all rejections and bases for continued viability; follow procedures in MPEP § 706.07(a) and §§ 716–716.10 for affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.
